Let’s take a closer look at Chapter 10—Hope and Uncertainty: Rwanda Today and the Ongoing Journey.
Decades after the genocide, Rwanda stands as a country transformed, though not untouched by its past. If you walk the streets of Kigali today, you’ll notice how clean and orderly everything seems. The economy’s on the rise, the government feels stable, and tourists flock to the national parks. They come to see the mountain gorillas, and they can’t help but remark on just how far Rwanda’s come.
But if you look a little deeper, you’ll find that the past still lingers. Survivors gather every year, not just to remember and mourn, but to hold each other up. The government’s focus on unity has definitely brought stability—there’s no denying that. Still, there’s a quiet sense of unease. Some people worry that talking openly about the past isn’t really encouraged, and that questioning the official story just isn’t an option. It’s as if some of those deep wounds have only been covered up—not truly healed.
Picture a young woman, born after the genocide. She listens to her parents’ stories, trying to understand, balancing curiosity with fear. She wants to know what happened, but she’s just as determined to build a life that isn’t defined by tragedy. She throws herself into her studies, dreams of becoming a doctor, and imagines a future where Rwanda is recognized for its strength—not its suffering.
Out in the countryside, there’s an old man tending his fields. He’s grateful for the peace that’s returned, but he can’t help but be a little wary. He remembers the days when neighbors turned against each other, and he prays his grandchildren will never have to face that same fear.
The truth is, healing is never really finished. Every generation has to figure out for themselves how to remember, how to forgive, and how to build a society where violence isn’t the answer. The lessons from Rwanda—they’re universal, but also deeply personal. They remind us that the capacity for both good and evil lives in every community, and in every single heart.
So, if there’s one thing to take away from Rwanda’s story, it’s that it isn’t just about tragedy. It’s a story of resilience, of courage, and of people fighting every day to create meaning after unimaginable horror. In a way, it’s a story that belongs to all of us—a warning, a hope, and a call to remember…and to act.
